answer.rationale: Binding constraints dominate: the primary contract lapses in 14 days with no auto-renew, and the line is at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer. That combination rules out switch_primary_vendor this cycle (memory_c2's fast, clean onboarding was achieved without a hard cliff or a capacity-constrained line, so it does not transfer) and rules out defer_decision (memory_c5's month-to-month fallback presupposed a non-critical service that kept running; here deferral means supply simply stops). add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right structural answer to concentration risk but does nothing for the 18% mandate and does not cover the expiring primary. That leaves negotiate_terms as the only move that both preserves continuity (memory_c1) and can touch TCO. Critically, the incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle \u2014 which directly contradicts the lever memory_c4 credits (benchmarking moving them on price and terms). So I want the c4 source record to see whether the movement came from benchmarking pressure per se or from some condition no longer present, and the c6 record to check whether the volume pricing unlocked by a multi-year commitment was genuinely a separate lever from reopening current-cycle price, and what scope guarantees actually held. If c6 holds up, the play is a term-structure and payment-terms deal (committed volume, non-price levers) rather than a price reopening. Deliberately guarded scale: I will pursue a short bridge or staged-reduction structure rather than a long lock-in, because an 18% cut is unlikely to be fully recoverable from the incumbent alone and a multi-year commitment signed under cliff pressure would foreclose the cheaper switch and the dual-source qualification I want available next cycle \u2014 that is the main downstream value risk here. If verification undercuts both c4 and c6, the fallback is a minimal continuity extension now and vendor qualification next review, accepting that the 18% target slips rather than putting a bufferless line at risk.
